sections.heading: Scheduling around a roster rather than an evening
paragraphs: A standard tutoring arrangement assumes a weekday evening that is reliably free. In a community where a significant share of households work airport and logistics rosters, that assumption fails every few weeks, and the usual result is a cancelled session, then another, then a quiet end to the arrangement. The fix is to design around the roster rather than hoping it cooperates.

Three things make it work. Slots are agreed a month ahead against the published roster rather than week by week. Weekend mornings and early weekday mornings are treated as normal options rather than as fallbacks, which suits a student who is awake anyway and a parent who is not. And the student holds the arrangement themselves from about fourteen upwards, with session notes going to the parent so nothing depends on being in the house at the time.

Online delivery is what makes all three possible. A visiting tutor needs a fixed route and a fixed evening to make the economics work, and a 06:30 session before school is not something anyone will drive to Dubai South for. IB Gram does not place tutors in UAE homes in any event; lessons are one-to-one over live video, which means the slot can follow the roster instead of the roster having to accommodate a car journey.

A note on the student's side of this. Teenagers in roster households often take on more domestic responsibility than their classmates, including younger siblings after school, and that is usually invisible to the school. It is worth naming it when a tutoring plan is set, because it changes which hour is realistically free and whether homework between sessions should be ten minutes or forty. A plan built on an hour that does not exist fails in the third week, and the fix is almost always to shorten the session and raise the frequency rather than to insist on the original slot.

sections.heading: Getting started from Emaar South
paragraphs: Send three things before booking anything: the most recent marked script, the exact syllabus code and tier from the examination entry, and the dates of the next school assessment and the school's internal deadlines. For a Diploma student, add the current predicted grades if the school has issued them. Those items let a tutor arrive with an opinion rather than a questionnaire.

The first session is diagnostic. The tutor reads the marked script with the student, question by question, and separates four different problems that look identical on a report: content not known, technique not trained, timing lost under pressure, and confidence gone. Each needs different work, and spending a term on the wrong one is the most common waste of money in this market. You receive a written summary.

Then three honest limits. We do not promise grades, points totals or prediction changes. We do not place tutors in homes anywhere in the UAE, so if in-person teaching is what you want we are the wrong provider. We do not supply board past papers or mark schemes, since those belong to the boards and schools hold the official versions. And where a tier decision or an entry deadline has already passed, we will say plainly what is still available rather than selling hours against a result that is already fixed.

A final word on what to expect in the first month. Week one is the diagnostic. Weeks two and three teach against whatever the script showed, with homework pinned to the next school assessment. Week four is normally a timed piece so that progress is measured on something marked rather than on an impression. You get a written note after every session, and a review at six weeks that either confirms the plan or changes it. If the marks have not moved by then we will change the tutor or the diagnosis rather than recommending more hours of the same arrangement.

process.title: Send the entry details
process.description: The syllabus code and tier for each subject, taken from the examination entry rather than from memory. For a Diploma student, the subject levels and any predicted grades issued. These determine which papers, mark schemes and content a tutor should be working from.

process.title: Diagnostic from a marked script
process.description: One online hour reading the most recent marked work with the student, question by question, to establish whether the problem is content, technique, timing or confidence. You receive a written summary naming which, and what work follows from it.

process.title: Check what is still changeable
process.description: Before anything is bought, we identify which decisions remain open: a tier change before the entry deadline, an unfinished internal assessment, a mathematics route still switchable, a prediction that new evidence could move. Those have the highest return per hour.

process.title: Fix slots against the roster
process.description: Sessions are placed a month ahead against your published shift pattern, including weekend mornings and early starts where weekday evenings are unreliable. The student holds the arrangement from around fourteen upwards, with notes copied to you.

process.title: Review on marked school work
process.description: Every four to six weeks, progress is measured on something a teacher marked, not on how sessions felt. If the marks have not moved, the tutor or the diagnosis changes rather than the number of hours increasing.

whyPoints.title: Mechanics explained before the deadline
whyPoints.description: Tier ceilings, prediction timing, entry deadlines and post-results windows are the decisions that actually determine a result, and most of them close before anyone starts revising. Understanding them early is worth more than extra hours later.

whyPoints.title: A diagnosis, not a subscription
whyPoints.description: The first session reads a marked script and names which of four problems you have. Content, technique, timing and lost confidence look identical on a report card and need completely different work, and getting it wrong costs a term.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling that survives a roster
whyPoints.description: Slots are planned a month ahead against shift patterns, with weekend and early-morning options treated as normal. Online delivery is what makes that possible; a driving route cannot accommodate a 06:30 session in Dubai South.

whyPoints.title: Figures you can trace
whyPoints.description: Every AED rate here names its publisher and the month it was collected. Every board date names the board that published it. Where a date or threshold could not be verified, this page says so rather than filling the gap.

whyPoints.title: What we will not claim
whyPoints.description: No grade promises, no prediction guarantees, no invented success rates, no accreditation from KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and no UAE office. Where a decision has already closed, we say so instead of selling hours against it.

faqs.question: What is the highest grade a Cambridge Core candidate can be awarded?
faqs.answer: A C. Cambridge IGCSE Core entries are graded C to G, and Extended entries A* to E, so a student entered for Core cannot be awarded above a C however well they perform in the examination. The tier is chosen by the school and submitted as part of the entry, which means the ceiling is set before any paper is opened. If your child is aiming at an A or B, or at a sixth form that requires one, the entry has to be Extended, and that decision has a deadline.

faqs.question: Can a Core entry be changed to Extended partway through Year 11?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, up to the board's entry deadline, and it is worth asking. The deadline depends on which series the school enters for: a Cambridge June entry closes in the spring, months before the papers, and a November entry closes over the preceding summer, with the exact date on the statement of entry. Ask the department in writing which tier your child is entered for and what evidence would support a move. Most will name a mark on a specific paper, which gives a measurable target rather than an argument.

faqs.question: Who decides my son's predicted grades and what are they based on?
faqs.answer: The school does, not the examination board. Predictions are the department's professional judgement built from work already completed: mocks, internal assessments, class assessments and observed trajectory. They matter because conditional university offers are made against them before any final result exists. The timing catches families out, because work left unfinished in the first Diploma year shapes a prediction issued in the second. Revision in the final term cannot retrospectively improve the evidence a prediction was based on.

faqs.question: What can we do if a predicted grade looks too low?
faqs.answer: Produce evidence rather than argue. Ask which specific pieces of work the prediction rests on, and ask what would need to change for it to be reviewed. Schools generally answer both questions directly, and the answer is usually a mark on a named assessment. A student who then produces a markedly stronger piece of assessed work has given the department something to act on. A parent disputing a judgement without new evidence has not, and the conversation rarely moves.

faqs.question: Why can't we just aim for last year's grade boundary?
faqs.answer: Because boundaries are set after each session, once the board has seen how candidates performed on that particular paper. They move so that a grade keeps the same meaning from one series to the next, which means last June's figure tells you nothing reliable about the next paper. Aiming at a boundary also trains students to stop collecting marks, which is the opposite of good examination technique. Use the mark scheme instead: it shows where every mark sits in an answer.

faqs.question: Can a remark lower my daughter's mark?
faqs.answer: Yes, which is why the decision deserves thought rather than reflex. A clerical check only confirms that marks were added and recorded correctly and carries little risk. A review of marking means the script is considered again against the mark scheme, and the outcome can be a lower mark as well as a higher one. Both routes are initiated by the school rather than the candidate, both carry a fee, and both have windows measured in weeks from results publication, so speak to the examinations officer immediately.

faqs.question: When are the November resit papers and results?
faqs.answer: For Pearson Edexcel International GCSE, the November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026, and results reach students in the January that follows: the November 2025 results landed on 22 January 2026. For context on summer turnaround, June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August and students on 20 August 2026. Cambridge runs the same two sittings for candidates here, June and November, with November functioning as the resit route. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so check the live official timetable rather than relying on a restated date, including on this page.

faqs.question: Does Applications and Interpretation close off engineering?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it depends entirely on the university. A number of engineering, physics, mathematics and quantitative economics programmes specify Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level, in their published entry requirements and will not treat the other course as equivalent. Others accept either. The only reliable method is to read the requirement pages for the four or five courses your child is actually considering, including UAE institutions, and to do it in the first Diploma year while a switch is still realistic.

faqs.question: How late can a student switch between the two maths courses?
faqs.answer: Early in the first Diploma year is realistic; after that the content diverges quickly and a switch becomes progressively less practical. Analysis and Approaches builds algebraic technique, proof and calculus; Applications and Interpretation builds modelling, statistics and technology use. A student a term into one course has already missed foundation work in the other. Where the route no longer matches the target course, the honest answer is sometimes that the target needs revisiting rather than that catch-up will fix it.

faqs.question: How does a weak internal assessment limit a Diploma subject grade?
faqs.answer: Arithmetically. Each Diploma subject grade is assembled from external components and an internal assessment, with the weights fixed by the subject guide. If the investigation carries a fifth of the subject, a student who submits weak work has removed a proportion of the available marks before papers begin, and revision cannot recover them. This is why finishing an investigation properly in the first Diploma year is a better purchase than extra revision in the final term, at the same hourly rate.

faqs.question: Can lessons fit an airline or logistics roster?
faqs.answer: Yes, and designing for it from the start works far better than hoping a weekday evening holds. Slots are agreed a month ahead against the published roster, weekend mornings and early weekday starts are treated as normal options rather than fallbacks, and from around fourteen the student holds the arrangement themselves with session notes copied to you. Online delivery is what makes this possible: nobody would drive to Dubai South for a 06:30 session, and IB Gram does not place tutors in UAE homes in any case.

faqs.question: Will someone come to the house in Emaar South?
faqs.answer: No. Home visits are a service IB Gram operates only in India, and every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. For this community the online format solves two problems at once. It removes a long drive from the far south of the city, which is what otherwise limits your choice to tutors willing to make that journey, and it allows the session to sit wherever the roster leaves a gap rather than only in a fixed weekday evening slot.

faqs.question: Do you supply past papers and mark schemes?
faqs.answer: No, and you should be cautious of anyone who does. Past papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables and subject guides belong to the examination boards, and reproducing or distributing them is a copyright matter. Schools hold the official versions and the boards publish what is intended for public use. What a tutor can legitimately do is work through material your school has provided, teach a student how to read a mark scheme properly, and point you to the official source for anything else.

faqs.question: Is there any point starting ten weeks before papers?
faqs.answer: Yes, provided the work changes shape. Ten weeks is not enough to learn a syllabus, and attempting it displaces the practice that actually moves marks. What works is a diagnostic from the most recent mock analysed question by question, timed papers at real length marked against the published scheme, and an error log the student maintains. That typically recovers marks lost to technique and timing rather than to ignorance, and we will say which of those your child's script shows.

faqs.question: What will IB Gram refuse to do for a family here?
faqs.answer: We will not promise a grade, a points total or a change to a predicted grade. We will not send a tutor to a UAE address. We will not write, edit to completion or supply any part of an internal assessment, Extended Essay or coursework. We will not distribute board papers or mark schemes. And we hold no accreditation, licence or partnership from KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, so you will not see that implied anywhere on this site.

dubai/emaar-south.closingHeading: Find out what is still changeable
dubai/emaar-south.closingBody: Most of what decides a result in this community is settled before anyone starts revising: the tier on an entry, whether an internal assessment was finished properly, which mathematics course was chosen, and what evidence a prediction rests on. Send the syllabus codes and tiers, the latest marked script and the school's internal deadlines, and one diagnostic hour online will tell you which of those remain open and which are already fixed. Where a decision has closed, we will say so plainly rather than selling hours against a result that cannot move, and where it is still open we will tell you exactly what work would change it.

dubai/emirates-hills.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach IB Diploma and IGCSE subjects to students at the schools Emirates Hills families use. What distinguishes the arrangement is not the subject list but the scheduling: fixed slots chosen around a real school run, with the length of each session set by the hour it occupies.

intro.heading: The afternoon, hour by hour, in a villa community built around a golf course
paragraphs: Emirates Hills is a low-density villa community wrapped around the Montgomerie golf course, with controlled entry, long internal roads and plots far enough apart that nobody walks anywhere. Two secondary schools sit on or beside its edges, and plenty of households send children further afield — into Al Barsha, Al Sufouh, Jumeirah or Dubai Hills — which means the family's afternoon is governed by whichever route is longest rather than by whichever is nearest.

That produces a scheduling problem with a shape unlike a tower community's. In an apartment building the constraint is space. Here the constraint is time and vehicles. A household with three children at three schools has three finish times, usually inside a forty-five-minute spread, and one or two drivers covering them. Whoever is collected last sets the hour at which the house becomes calm, and every tutoring arrangement in the family is downstream of that single figure.

Most Dubai secondary schools finish somewhere between 2.45pm and 3.30pm, and you should confirm your own child's time rather than assume, because it varies by school, by year group and by day. What follows the bell is the part families underestimate: a bus or car that waits, a route that crosses the afternoon peak, a gate, an internal drive, then food. The gap between the final bell and a child genuinely able to think is routinely two hours, and on an Al Barsha run it can be more.

Layered on top of that is the activity timetable, which in this community is substantial and mostly sits between four and six in the afternoon. Swimming, tennis, football academies, music and golf all compete for exactly the window a tutor would otherwise occupy. Families who try to insert a lesson into that window end up cancelling it a fortnight in, then concluding that the tutoring did not work. The tutoring was fine; the slot was wrong.

There is a less obvious cost in a gated villa community, and it falls on in-home arrangements specifically. A visitor has to be registered at the gate, driven along internal roads to a villa that may be several minutes from the entrance, and let in by someone. Multiply that by two trips a week and the travel inside an in-home rate stops being nominal. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 an hour, with independent tutors quoting up to AED 500, and the geography here is part of why.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Lessons here are one-to-one over live video, in Gulf Standard Time slots chosen from the family's real clock rather than from a provider's preference. The practical advantage in Emirates Hills is simple: the session can start at 7.10pm because that is when the last child is home and fed, it can move by twenty minutes when a match runs long, and nothing about it depends on a gate.

dubai/emirates-hills.programmesIntro: Emirates Hills households sit across the full range of programmes, often with siblings on different ones. The notes below say what each programme does to an evening, which is the relevant question on this page.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across six groups with three at Higher Level, plus a 4,000-word Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge with an essay and an exhibition, and CAS. Scored out of 45 with 24 needed to pass. Every subject carries an internal assessment produced largely outside lesson time.
programmes.countryNote: The heaviest programme on a household's evenings. A Diploma student with three live internal assessments has long-horizon work that competes with every activity in the week, and the honest advice for a DP2 autumn is often to drop one commitment rather than add a tutor. Where a session is right, one hour on a fixed evening beats two scattered hours.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Two years per subject against a published syllabus code, assessed by terminal papers with practical or alternative-to-practical components in the sciences. Most Cambridge subjects split into Core and Extended tiers with different grade ceilings, decided by the school at entry.
programmes.countryNote: The two IGCSE years are where a family can most easily get the scheduling right, because the work is content-led and responds well to a short regular slot. Two forty-five-minute sessions a week at a sensible hour outperform one ninety-minute session at a bad one, which is the opposite of what most families buy.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson A Level
programmes.description: Three or four subjects in depth, assessed by terminal papers with practical endorsement in some sciences depending on the specification. No compulsory breadth and no core, which concentrates all the risk into a small number of papers.
programmes.countryNote: With three subjects, the week has more room in it than a Diploma week does, which makes an early-evening slot genuinely available for A Level students in this community. It also means a single under-taught module costs proportionally more, so the regular slot is better spent on depth than on general revision.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Five years assessed against criteria A to D in each subject group, with a Personal Project in the final year and marks reported as criterion levels rather than percentages. The command terms used are the ones the Diploma will use later.
programmes.countryNote: The years where scheduling habits are formed, and the best time to establish a fixed weekly slot that a student owns rather than one a parent enforces. A Year 9 student who has run a standing session and a retrieval routine for a year arrives in the Diploma with the only study skill that actually scales.

dubai/emirates-hills.subjectsIntro: For each subject below, what it needs in terms of time rather than content: how long a productive session is, how often, and whether it tolerates a late slot.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: Tolerates a late slot better than almost anything else, because the work is procedural and a tired student can still practise technique. Two short sessions a week beat one long one: method-mark discipline and non-calculator fluency both respond to frequency rather than duration.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: At Higher Level this needs the best hour available, not the leftover one. Proof and series work demands sustained concentration, so a 6.30pm session on a day with no activity after it is worth considerably more than a 7.45pm session after a swim squad.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics work splits neatly into shorter blocks, which makes it one of the easier Diploma subjects to schedule around a busy week. The exploration is the exception: it needs a longer session once, early, to fix the question rather than weekly nibbling.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Pearson 4PH1 and IB Physics)
subjects.description: Numerical practice survives a late slot; six-mark explanation work does not, because writing a causal chain in physics language needs a fresh brain. Put the explanation work in the earlier of two weekly slots and the calculation practice in the later one.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Pearson 4CH1 and IB Chemistry)
subjects.description: The descriptive memorisation — qualitative analysis, colours, precipitates — is daily fifteen-minute work rather than session work, and it is best set as a routine and checked rather than taught. Session time is better spent on mechanisms and on the data-based question.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Pearson 4BI1 and IB Biology)
subjects.description: Wide syllabus, terminal paper, so retention is the problem and frequency beats duration. A twenty-minute retrieval routine three times a week does more than an extra hour of teaching, and a session is best used to set and check that routine rather than to re-cover content.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature (Cambridge 0500 / Pearson 4EA1 / English A)
subjects.description: The least late-slot-tolerant subject in the house. Directed writing, the individual oral and the Higher Level essay all require composition under time, which a tired student cannot do well. If a family has one good hour in the week, this is the subject that should get it.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Management
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy in Economics and case-study evaluation in Business Management both work in shorter blocks. The internal assessments need a longer session at the start for scoping and then brief check-ins, which fits a crowded week better than most Diploma components.

subjects.name: History and Geography
subjects.description: Source evaluation and case-study building are reading-led, so the session is most useful as a structure-and-feedback meeting on work already done. That makes them good candidates for the latest slot in the week, since the heavy lifting happens outside it.

subjects.name: Second languages: French, Spanish, Arabic and Hindi
subjects.description: Speaking practice needs frequency above all, so three twenty-minute conversations a week beat one hour. These are also the sessions most tolerant of a short, late or slightly chaotic slot, which makes them the easiest thing to fit into a Thursday evening.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Not weekly work. These need two or three longer sessions at the right moments — scoping the question before research, structuring before the first draft, feedback after it — which means booking them against school deadlines rather than fitting them into a standing slot.

subjects.name: Arabic and Islamic Education as mandatory subjects
subjects.levels: All year groups in Dubai private schools
subjects.description: Mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, with instructional time calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit and KHDA advising at least 25 minutes per mandatory-subject lesson. They occupy weekly school time, which reduces the free study periods a parent may be assuming exist.

sections.heading: What an Emirates Hills parent is really asking, which is 'when'
paragraphs: Families here are not usually short of options and are rarely short of willingness. The question that actually decides whether tutoring works in this community is when the lesson can be, and it is almost never asked first. A provider offers a 4pm or 5pm slot because that is when tutors prefer to teach, a parent accepts it because it sounds reasonable, and the arrangement collapses within a month for reasons that have nothing to do with teaching.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. Most Dubai secondary schools finish between 2.45pm and 3.30pm — check your own, because it varies by school, year group and day. Add a bus that waits and loops, a route across the afternoon peak, a controlled gate, an internal drive and a meal, and the honest figure for a child able to concentrate is two hours after the bell on a good day. On an Al Barsha or Al Sufouh run it is longer, and the variance between days is wide enough that a fixed early slot will miss regularly.

Then the activity timetable, which in this community is dense and mostly occupies four to six in the afternoon. Swim squads, tennis coaching, football academies, music lessons and golf all sit exactly where a tutor would. A family trying to insert a session into that band is choosing between two things the child is committed to, and the tutoring loses because it is the newer commitment.

So the sequence that works is backwards from the constraints. Write down each child's finish time and route. Write down every fixed commitment in the week. Find what is actually left. Then choose which subject gets the best remaining hour and which gets the shorter, later one. Families who do this in September keep their arrangements all year; families who buy a slot first spend the year rescheduling it.

sections.heading: From the final bell to a child at a desk
paragraphs: This is the table families in this community should build for themselves in September, and almost nobody does. It has four columns: where the child goes to school, when the day ends, how they travel, and the hour at which they are realistically at a desk having eaten. The fourth column is the only one that matters for scheduling, and it is always later than the parent's estimate.

Several factors stretch the gap in Emirates Hills specifically. School buses collect across several communities in Emirates Living and the surrounding areas, so a bus-borne child reaches home noticeably later than a car-borne sibling at the same school. The community's controlled entry adds minutes at the gate during the afternoon return. And the internal roads are long: a villa several minutes' drive from the entrance adds a real amount to every arrival.

The figures in the table below are planning assumptions rather than published facts, offered so a family has somewhere to start. Replace each one with your own measurement over a fortnight — note the actual time your child sat down, on five consecutive days — and schedule from the latest of those five rather than the average. A slot built on an average will fail on two days in five, which is enough for a student to conclude that tutoring is something that keeps getting cancelled.

The payoff for doing this properly is large and immediate. A session placed at the right hour is attended, and a session that is attended builds the habit that makes the next two years easier. A session placed half an hour too early is cancelled or arrives with a child who is hungry, hot and unable to think, and parents then pay for both the session and the conclusion that it did not help.

sections.heading: Three children, three finish times, one driver
paragraphs: A single-child household in this community has a scheduling problem. A three-child household has a logistics problem, and it is usually solved by whoever has the strongest claim on the vehicle rather than by whoever most needs a tutor. That is worth naming, because the academic consequence is that the middle child's session is the one that gets dropped.

The pattern we see repeatedly: an eldest in DP2 whose sessions are protected because the exams are visible and imminent, a youngest in Year 7 whose activities are protected because they are new and enjoyed, and a Year 10 in the middle whose IGCSE course has quietly started and whose session is the flexible one. Two years later the eldest has left, the youngest is fine, and the middle child is the one with thin strands and a tier decision nobody argued about.

The fix is structural rather than motivational. Do not put all three children's sessions on the same two evenings. Spread them across the week so that each child has a slot that does not compete with a sibling's, and so that a single bad evening costs one session rather than three. Accept that this means tutoring appears on four evenings rather than two, which sounds worse and is in fact considerably lighter per evening.

The second part of the fix is to schedule the middle child first. Whoever has the least visible deadline is the one whose slot should be chosen before anybody else's, because theirs is the slot that will otherwise be assembled from leftovers. The eldest's exam urgency will find a slot regardless; the youngest's activities will be protected by enthusiasm. The middle child's two IGCSE years will not defend themselves.

sections.heading: Activities are the constraint, not the problem
paragraphs: It would be easy to write this section as an argument for fewer activities. That is not the advice. Sustained commitment to a sport or an instrument is one of the few things that reads honestly in a university application, it is the main source of CAS evidence for a Diploma student, and it is often the part of the week a child actually wants. The point is that it is a fixed constraint, and a tutoring plan has to be built around it rather than in competition with it.

What that means in practice is identifying which commitments are genuinely immovable and which are not. A swim squad with a coach and a fixed lane time is immovable. A tennis lesson booked privately can usually move by a day. A music lesson at home can move by thirty minutes. Families who treat all commitments as equally fixed end up with no slots at all; families who audit them usually find one evening more than they thought they had.

The second practical step is to accept what a post-activity slot can and cannot do. A child home from football at 6.30pm, fed at 7pm and at a desk at 7.30pm can practise mathematics technique, drill vocabulary or review a marked paper. They cannot write a Higher Level English essay or work through a proof. That is not laziness; it is how attention works at the end of a long day in a hot climate.

So the allocation rule is simple. The best hour in the week goes to the subject that needs composition or sustained reasoning. The post-activity slots get procedural work, retrieval and review. A family that reverses this spends the good hour on vocabulary drill and then wonders why the English grade has not moved.

sections.heading: What the hour of the day does to a lesson
paragraphs: Session length is sold as a product — the sixty-minute lesson, the ninety-minute lesson — when it should be a function of the hour it occupies and the work being done. An hour at 5pm with a rested child is a different object from an hour at 8pm after a swim squad, and pretending otherwise is why some families conclude that their child is bad at a subject when they are actually tired at it.

Three things change with the hour. Working-memory load tolerance falls, so multi-step reasoning becomes expensive late in the evening. Writing stamina falls faster than reading stamina, which is why composition work must sit earlier. And error-correction tolerance falls: a tired student who is told they have made a mistake disengages where a rested one would be curious, so marked-work review late in the evening needs to be shorter and gentler.

There is also a floor below which a session stops being worth the disruption. Thirty minutes is enough for language conversation, vocabulary testing, a worked example set, or reviewing one marked question properly. It is not enough to start a new topic, and a tutor who begins teaching new content in the last twenty minutes of a late session is wasting the family's money whether or not the clock says an hour was delivered.

The table below sets out what each slot can carry. It is written as guidance for a family deciding what to buy, not as a rule we impose: a student who genuinely works better at nine o'clock exists and should be scheduled accordingly. The purpose is to stop households buying a sixty-minute composition session at 8pm and then concluding the tutor was ineffective.

sections.heading: Why a tutor at the gate costs more than the rate suggests
paragraphs: Families here do ask about in-home tutoring, and it exists. The published market rate reflects what travel costs: Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 an hour, and independent tutors quote up to AED 500. For comparison, a qualified subject tutor working online in this market is published at AED 150 to 300 by Unitors and others, with exam-year specialists at AED 200 to 450 or above per Bestimate and AED 270 at TutorChase.

In a gated, low-density community the gap between those bands is not arbitrary. A visitor has to be registered at the entry, driven along internal roads, and received at a villa that may be several minutes from the gate. Two visits a week, across a school year, is a substantial amount of unpaid time for a tutor, and it is recovered in the rate whether or not it is itemised. It also narrows the pool sharply: the tutors who will do it are the ones who live close enough, which is not the same set as the ones who know your child's syllabus code.

There is a second cost that lands on the family rather than the tutor. An in-home slot cannot move easily. When a match runs long or a bus is late, a visitor is already en route and the session is either lost or delivered to a child who has just walked through the door. An online slot shifts by twenty minutes with a message, which across a year in this community is the difference between thirty sessions delivered and twenty-two.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Lessons here are one-to-one over live video, which is why the scheduling flexibility this page keeps describing is available at all. The honest statement of the trade-off is that a family loses the presence of an adult in the room and gains both a wider specialist pool and a slot that bends instead of breaking.

sections.heading: Study leave and the exam fortnight, when mornings finally work
paragraphs: Everything on this page about late slots and short sessions applies to term time. For a few weeks a year the constraint lifts entirely, and families should plan for that rather than drifting through it. During study leave and the exam period a student is at home in the morning, which is when timed papers should be sat, because that is when the real papers are sat and because concentration is at its best.

The useful structure for that fortnight is a full paper at the hour the real paper falls, followed the same day or the next by error analysis on what was lost. That is a ninety-minute session plus a forty-five-minute one, and it is worth considerably more than three hours of teaching in the same week. By study leave the teaching should be finished; what remains is execution, and execution is practised under conditions rather than explained.

Error analysis is the part families skip and it is where the marks are. The question is not which answers were wrong but why: content not known, content known and not retrieved, command term misread, method not stated, time mismanaged, or question misread entirely. Those six causes need six different responses, and a student who can classify their own lost marks fixes them far faster than one who simply redoes the paper.

Worth noting for Cambridge candidates specifically: every Cambridge centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, and it adds that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong version. Confirm the zone with the school's exams officer and build the study-leave schedule from that timetable rather than from any other copy.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the shortened day, and the two-month summer
paragraphs: Two periods each year change the clock completely, and both are predictable enough to plan for in advance rather than improvising through. During Ramadan school days are shortened, which brings children home earlier and makes an afternoon slot briefly available, but energy through the day is lower and the natural working window moves to after Iftar in many households.

The arrangement that works is to agree the Ramadan schedule a fortnight before it begins rather than in its first week. For most families that means either an early-afternoon slot while the shortened day lasts, or a post-Iftar slot in the evening, chosen per child rather than per household. Post-Iftar scheduling is markedly easier online than with a visitor crossing the city late, which is one of the clearer practical advantages of the format in this community.

The long summer is the other. Families in Emirates Hills typically travel for part of it, and the two-month gap does real damage to subjects that depend on retention — Biology, languages, anything with a vocabulary bank. The proportionate response is not a full summer schedule but a light one: one short session a week, or a retrieval routine the student runs alone with a monthly check, aimed specifically at the material that decays.

Where a family travels, sessions either pause by agreement or continue at whatever hour the destination timezone allows, since nothing about the arrangement requires anybody to be in the Emirates. The one thing worth avoiding is a complete two-month stop followed by a September restart in the middle of a new course, which is how a student arrives in Year 11 or DP2 behind on last year's material and new content at the same time.
bullets: Agree the Ramadan schedule a fortnight ahead, not in its first week

sections.heading: What the hour should contain when there is only one hour
paragraphs: In a week this full, most families end up with one genuinely good hour per child, and the question of what goes into it matters more than the choice of tutor. The answer that works is almost never a lecture. A session built as explanation uses the student's best hour to make them a listener, which is the least valuable thing they can do with it.

A better shape is roughly: five minutes reviewing what was set and whether it was done, fifteen minutes of the student attempting something new with the tutor watching, fifteen minutes of correction and explanation aimed only at what went wrong, fifteen minutes of independent practice under observation, and five minutes agreeing what happens before the next session. The student works for most of it; the tutor intervenes.

The second thing the hour should contain is marking. A student who marks their own work against the official mark scheme while a tutor watches learns where marks sit, which transfers to every subject. A student who is told their mark learns their mark. We reference and link board papers and mark schemes on the official sites rather than reproducing them, because the official copy is the current one.

And the hour should end with something written down. In a household with three children and a driver, the note after the session is what makes the arrangement legible to a parent who was not in the room: what was covered, what was set, what to ask about. That note is also how a parent notices, by week six, that the same weakness keeps appearing, which is the signal to change the plan rather than to buy more hours.
bullets: The student should be working for most of the hour; the tutor intervenes

sections.heading: Starting from an Emirates Hills address
paragraphs: The first message that helps is a timetable rather than a description of the problem. For each child: school, year group, subjects, what time they get home on a normal day, and every fixed commitment in the week. That is enough to propose slots that will survive the term, which is a better starting point than agreeing a subject and then discovering there is nowhere to put it.

If you have the syllabus codes, send those too. If you do not, one email to the exams officer asking for the syllabus code, the tier and the series for each subject in writing is worth sending regardless, because it determines whether the past papers at home are the right ones and, for Cambridge subjects, whether a Core entry has quietly capped a grade at 5.

Then a free trial lesson with the specialist who would actually teach the subject, placed in the slot you would really use rather than in a convenient demonstration slot. No card details, no commitment. Trialling at the wrong hour tells you very little; trialling at 7.15pm on a Wednesday after football tells you exactly what you need to know.

After that, a proposed schedule with the reasoning attached: which subject gets the best hour and why, which slots are forty-five minutes rather than sixty, and which evening is deliberately left empty. If the honest answer is that the week has no room and something should come out rather than go in, we will say that. A session a child resents, squeezed into a slot that was already taken, teaches them that help is a burden.

faqs.question: What is the earliest a session can realistically start in Emirates Hills?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the route. A child at a school on or beside Emirates Living is often home by 3.45pm, which makes a 5pm session genuinely viable if no activity follows. A child collected from Al Barsha at around 3.15pm faces the afternoon peak and is rarely at a desk, fed, before 5.15pm or later, which makes 6.30pm the first slot worth offering. Measure your own child's desk time over five consecutive days and schedule from the latest of those five, not the average.

faqs.question: Why did our last tutoring arrangement keep getting cancelled?
faqs.answer: Almost always because the slot was placed in the four-to-six window, which in this community is occupied by swimming, tennis, football, music and golf. A session inserted there competes with a commitment the child already has, and the newer commitment loses. The usual outcome is that the family concludes the tutoring did not work, when in fact it was never delivered consistently. Audit the week's fixed commitments first, then choose a slot from what is genuinely left.

faqs.question: Is one long session a week better than two short ones?
faqs.answer: For most subjects, no. Mathematics method discipline, non-calculator fluency, language speaking and retrieval across a wide syllabus all respond to frequency rather than duration, so two forty-five-minute sessions generally beat one ninety-minute block. The exceptions are the things that need sustained reasoning or composition — Higher Level mathematics proof work, English essays — which deserve one properly protected hour. Two shorter slots are also easier to defend across a term in a household with several children.

faqs.question: Does the time of day really change how much a lesson achieves?
faqs.answer: Yes, and in predictable ways. Tolerance for multi-step reasoning falls through the evening, writing stamina falls faster than reading stamina, and a tired student responds worse to being corrected. An hour at 5.30pm can carry new content and composition; an hour at 8pm is better spent on technique drill, vocabulary testing or reviewing one marked question properly. Buying a sixty-minute essay-writing session at 8pm and concluding the tutor was ineffective is a common and avoidable mistake.

faqs.question: We have three children at three schools. How should we spread sessions?
faqs.answer: Across four evenings rather than two, with one evening deliberately left empty, and schedule the child with the least visible deadline first. The pattern we see is that the eldest in DP2 gets protected because exams are imminent, the youngest's activities get protected because they are enjoyed, and the Year 10 in the middle has the flexible slot that quietly disappears. Two years later that middle child is the one with thin strands and a tier decision nobody argued about.

faqs.question: Should we cut activities to make room for tutoring?
faqs.answer: Rarely, and not as a first move. Sustained commitment to a sport or an instrument is one of the few things that reads honestly in a university application and is the main source of CAS evidence for a Diploma student. The better approach is to audit which commitments are genuinely immovable — a squad with a fixed lane time is, a privately booked lesson usually is not — because most households find one evening more than they thought they had once they look properly.

faqs.question: Does a tutor come to our villa in Emirates Hills?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. In-home tutoring does exist in Dubai at published rates of AED 180 to 350 an hour, with independents quoting to AED 500, and in a gated community the travel inside that rate is real: gate registration, a long internal drive and two unpaid journeys a week. It also narrows the tutor pool to whoever lives nearby, which is not the same group as those who know your child's syllabus code.

faqs.question: What happens when a match or rehearsal runs over?
faqs.answer: An online session moves by twenty or thirty minutes with a message, which across a school year is worth several delivered sessions. An in-home arrangement cannot do that, because the tutor is already travelling when the overrun happens, so the session is either lost or delivered to a child who has just walked through the door. That flexibility is the single most useful practical difference in a community where afternoons routinely overrun.

faqs.question: When should sessions move to mornings?
faqs.answer: During study leave, half-term and the exam fortnight, which is the only part of the year when mornings are available. That is also when they are most valuable: a full paper sat at the hour the real paper falls, followed by error analysis on what was lost, is worth more than three hours of teaching in the same week. By study leave the teaching should be finished, and what remains is execution, which is practised under real conditions rather than explained.

faqs.question: What should a tutor do with a marked past paper?
faqs.answer: Have the student classify their own lost marks by cause before any explanation: content not known, content known but not retrieved, command term misread, method not stated, time mismanaged, or question misread. Those six causes need six different responses, and a student who can sort their own errors fixes them far faster than one who simply redoes the paper. The student should also mark against the official scheme while the tutor watches, which teaches where marks sit.

faqs.question: How do sessions work during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: The schedule is agreed a fortnight before it begins rather than improvised in the first week. Shortened school days bring children home earlier, which briefly opens an afternoon slot, but energy through the day is lower and many households find a post-Iftar slot works better. The choice is best made per child rather than per household. Post-Iftar scheduling is considerably easier online than with a visitor crossing the city late in the evening.

faqs.question: Should tutoring continue through the summer?
faqs.answer: Lightly, and aimed at what actually decays. A two-month gap damages retention subjects most: Biology, languages, and anything with a vocabulary or definitions bank. The proportionate response is one short session a week, or a retrieval routine the student runs alone with a monthly check, rather than a full summer schedule. The arrangement to avoid is a complete stop followed by a September restart, which leaves a student behind on last year's material and meeting new content simultaneously.

faqs.question: What do tutors charge in this part of Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published figures as of October 2026: Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 to 52 an hour and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65 at the generalist end; Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200 for a qualified subject tutor online; TutorChase lists AED 270 and BartyED AED 650 at the specialist and premium end. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table puts in-home visits at AED 180 to 350 and exam-year specialists at AED 200 to 450 or above. Those are their figures; we quote after a free trial.

faqs.question: How do we know whether the slot is working rather than just happening?
faqs.answer: Look at the written note after each session and count two things: whether what was set last week was done, and whether the same weakness keeps appearing. If the set work is not being done, the problem is the slot or the load, not the teaching. If the same weakness recurs by week six, the plan should change rather than more hours being bought. Both signals are visible to a parent who was never in the room, which is the point of the note.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover two of our children in the same session?
faqs.answer: Not in the same session, and usually not usefully at all unless they are in the same year group sitting the same syllabus code. Two children at different levels in one hour means both receive half an hour, and in practice the quieter one receives less. Staggered slots on different evenings cost the same in hours and deliver substantially more, and they also mean a single disrupted evening costs one session rather than two.

faqs.question: What if our week genuinely has no room for a session?
faqs.answer: Then the honest answer is that something should come out before anything goes in, and we will say so. A Diploma student in DP2 with three live internal assessments, an Extended Essay deadline and four weekly commitments does not need a fifth. Sometimes the useful purchase is two sessions setting up a retrieval routine and a deadline calendar the student runs alone, rather than a standing weekly slot. A session a child resents teaches them that help is a burden.

intro.heading: The evening hour is the scarcest thing you will buy, so spend it on one thing
paragraphs: Look at a Dubai Diploma student's Tuesday. The bus drops them somewhere between 15:15 and 16:30 depending on the community. There is homework in six subjects, an internal assessment with a deadline, football or music on two or three evenings, a family that eats together, and a body that has been awake since six. Into that a parent adds a tutoring session, usually between 18:00 and 20:00 because that is when everyone is home. The hour exists. The question is what it is capable of.

It is capable of exactly one thing. A single topic taught properly. A single question type drilled until the pattern changes. One section of an internal assessment draft read against its criteria and discussed. A set of six past-paper questions marked and understood. What it cannot do is cover a term's backlog, prepare three subjects, or sit a full two-hour paper, and sessions that try end up as thirty minutes of chat and thirty minutes of skimming.

That constraint is not a weakness. A weekly hour with one clear objective, repeated for twelve weeks, is twelve things fixed, and twelve things is usually more than a Diploma student needs to move a grade band where the losses are habits. The failure mode of evening tutoring is not the length of the session; it is the absence of an objective. A tutor who arrives and asks what shall we do today has already spent fifteen minutes of a paid hour deciding.

The second thing this page is about is the hour itself. A 17:00 session and a 20:30 session are different products bought with the same money. At 17:00 a student is tired but still capable of new material; by 20:30 the only reliable work is consolidation, practice on something already known, or a conversation about a draft. A parent who books the convenient slot rather than the correct one is often paying full price for the weakest version of the session.

Gulf Standard Time is the third variable, and the one nobody mentions. Dubai sits four hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time, which means that a 19:00 Dubai slot is mid-afternoon in London, late evening in South Asia and the middle of the night in East Asia and Australia. That arithmetic decides which specialists can take your slot at all. It is also the honest reason a late Dubai evening can be covered by a strong subject specialist rather than whoever happens to be free locally.

Below: the evening hour by hour, the time-zone map, what one hour fixes per subject, why a 21:00 session is usually a poor purchase, how evening tutoring sits against the drive to a tuition centre, and what evening rates look like in AED at published 2026 market levels.

17:00 for new material; 20:00 and later for consolidation and practice

dubai/evening-ib-tutor.programmesIntro: An evening hour is used differently at each stage of the IB continuum, and the realistic objective for one session changes with the programme. These are the stages Dubai families book evening slots for.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. In an evening hour the realistic objectives are one topic, one question type or one section of a draft. Full timed papers belong to a longer weekend block, because a two-hour paper plus marking does not fit a school night.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai Diploma students typically carry homework across six subjects every night, and school deadlines for internal assessments are set locally rather than by the IB, so two students in the same emirate can be eight weeks apart on the same component. The evening objective should be set against the next dated thing in your own school's calendar.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups with four lettered criteria each, reported 1-8 per criterion. An evening hour here is well spent on criterion literacy: taking one task the school has marked and working out what separates the band awarded from the band above. That is a one-hour job with a visible outcome.
programmes.countryNote: Younger students in Dubai are often fresher at 16:30 than Diploma students are, because the homework load is lighter, so early evening slots are genuinely productive for Years 7 to 9. Year 10 and 11 students sit closer to the Diploma pattern, with activities and coursework competing for the same hours.

programmes.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
programmes.description: The exhibition with its three objects and commentary, the prescribed-title essay, and the 4,000-word Extended Essay with a school-appointed supervisor. These suit evening hours better than most people expect, because one hour is enough to interrogate a research question or test whether a section answers what it claims to.
programmes.countryNote: The Extended Essay supervisor is appointed by the Dubai school and signs the reflection sessions; a tutor works beside that and never in place of it. An evening hour spent asking whether the question can be answered in 4,000 words, two months before the first draft is due, saves considerably more time than it costs.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Transdisciplinary inquiry with no external examinations, ending in the Year 6 exhibition. Evening sessions for primary students should be short, 30 or 45 minutes, early rather than late, and focused on one skill: reading fluency, number facts or sentence structure. An hour after 19:00 is rarely productive at this age.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai primary families often ask for a 17:00 slot and then find homework and dinner collide with it. The 16:30 start, straight off the bus with a snack, works better in practice. Arabic is mandatory in Dubai private schools from the early years, so a non-Arab child may be carrying a second script alongside English literacy.

dubai/evening-ib-tutor.subjectsIntro: These are the Diploma subjects most often booked into evening slots, with the realistic objective for a single hour in each. The test of a good evening tutor is whether they can name that objective before the session rather than during it.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: An hour fits one technique to the point of fluency: integration by substitution, binomial expansion, one proof method. It does not fit a mixed paper. The most valuable evening objective is often method presentation, because unshown working costs marks that the student has already earned mathematically.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Questions are long and contextual, so an hour is best spent on two or three full questions read carefully rather than ten short ones. Statistics work suits the evening well; the modelling questions need more time than a school night allows and belong in a longer block.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: One hour is right for a single mechanism, one calculation type, or the evaluation section of an internal assessment draft. Energetics and equilibrium both reward short repeated practice. Significant figures and state symbols are a fifteen-minute fix that students keep failing to make, which makes them an ideal evening objective.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Extended-response explanation can be taught in an hour if the objective is the structure of the answer rather than the topic: claim, mechanism, consequence, with the physics named at each step. Uncertainty work for the internal assessment needs a longer sitting, because it cannot be rushed without being redone.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: An hour suits a set of unseen data-analysis questions, marked and discussed, which is the part of the paper students practise least. Terminology precision is another good single objective: a list of the near-synonyms the markscheme rejects, drilled once, changes answers permanently.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy is the best possible evening objective, because it is finite and visibly improvable: axes, labels, shift direction, new equilibrium marked. One commentary section can also be discussed in an hour. Writing a whole 800-word commentary cannot, and should not be attempted inside a session.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: One unseen extract analysed properly fills an hour. So does rehearsing one segment of the individual oral. What does not fit is a full Paper 1 under timed conditions, which needs a longer block, so the evening job is technique on a short text rather than exam simulation.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Source work suits the evening precisely: two sources, provenance analysed, cross-referenced, marked. The HL regional option benefits from a weekly hour spent building a bank of dated specifics, ten at a time, which is dull and is exactly the kind of task a fixed weekly slot makes happen.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: One tool applied to one piece of stimulus, done properly, is an hour well spent. The Higher Level pre-released case study rewards exactly this kind of incremental weekly work across months, which is the one place where an evening hour beats an occasional long block.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: An hour is enough to test whether an argument answers its prescribed title, which is the most common structural failure in the essay. Also enough to choose and justify one exhibition object. Students usually leave these sessions with fewer words written and a clearer idea of what they are arguing.

dubai/evening-ib-tutor.regionsIntro: Evening availability in Dubai is shaped by when the student gets home and what else is in the diary, not by where the tutor is. These are the communities evening requests most often come from and the realistic start time in each.

regions.name: Business Bay
regions.note: Apartment living with short school runs to the Downtown and Al Quoz corridors, so a 16:30 or 17:00 start is realistic. Parents working nearby are often home earlier than the emirate average, which makes the earlier slot easier to supervise than it is in the outer communities.

regions.name: Downtown Dubai
regions.note: Similar rhythm to Business Bay, with activities concentrated inside the community rather than across the city. The 17:00 slot survives well here. Diploma students in the final term often add a second weekly hour rather than lengthening the first.

regions.name: Dubai International Financial Centre
regions.note: Small residential population, mostly apartments, with students travelling to schools in Al Barsha, Jumeirah and Oud Metha. Return times vary widely by school bus route, so the practical approach is to fix the slot after the first week of term rather than before it.

regions.name: Dubai Creek Harbour
regions.note: Newer community with longer runs out towards Mirdif, Al Garhoud and Nad Al Sheba. Students frequently arrive home after 16:30, which pushes the useful start to 17:30 or later. Sibling pairs in consecutive hours are common here.

regions.name: Sobha Hartland
regions.note: Schools within or adjacent to the community, so early evening works unusually well. Families often take 16:30 for a younger child and 18:00 for a Diploma student, which online delivery handles without anyone travelling between the two.

regions.name: Meydan
regions.note: Villa community with school runs towards Nad Al Sheba and Dubai Hills. Activity schedules are heavy on weekday evenings, so the 19:00 and 19:30 slots are the ones that hold. Consolidation work suits those hours better than new material.

regions.name: Al Jaddaf
regions.note: Apartment community close to the creek with students spread across Oud Metha, Al Garhoud and Academic City schools. Study space is the main constraint, so a fixed desk and headphones matter more than the exact start time.

schoolClusters.note: Students we support attend these schools. Names are context for families comparing Diploma cohort sizes, subject availability and homework load, and imply no relationship with any school.

schoolClusters.city: Schools serving Business Bay, Downtown, Meydan and Al Jaddaf
schoolClusters.note: These schools serve the communities listed above. Their homework patterns and internal deadlines differ enough that an evening plan should be built from your own school's calendar rather than a generic Dubai one.

dubai/evening-ib-tutor.modesIntro: Three evening formats cover almost every Dubai request. All three run online, one-to-one, over live video with screen sharing, and all three end with a written note naming the next piece of work.

modes.title: Single weekly hour, one subject
modes.description: The standard arrangement: same tutor, same slot, one subject, one objective per session. Twelve weeks of this is twelve specific things fixed, which is usually enough to move a grade band where the losses are habits rather than missing content.

modes.title: Two short evenings instead of one long one
modes.description: Two 45-minute sessions on different evenings rather than one 90-minute session. Better for younger students and for anyone working on fluency rather than understanding, because short repeated contact beats one long sitting when the goal is automaticity.

modes.title: Weekly evening hour plus a weekend long block
modes.description: The hybrid that solves the evening hour's one real limitation. The weekday hour keeps content moving; a longer weekend block exists to sit a full timed paper and mark it, which a school night cannot hold. Progress is measured on the long blocks.

sections.heading: The Dubai evening, hour by hour: what each slot can actually carry
paragraphs: Treat the evening as four different products. From 16:30 a student is tired but still able to take in new material, which makes it the only slot where genuinely new content teaching works well. From 18:00 the household is busiest and the student is at their most distracted, but the hour is still strong for guided practice with the tutor watching. From 19:30 new material stops landing and the useful work becomes consolidation of something already half-known. After 21:00 very little survives to the next morning.

Most families book on convenience, which puts the majority of sessions into the 18:00 to 20:00 window, and that is why it is the most contested time in the emirate. The better approach is to match the objective to the hour. If the aim is to teach integration by substitution, book 16:30 or accept that the first attempt will need repeating. If the aim is to drill twenty short recall questions or discuss an internal assessment draft, a 20:00 slot is perfectly adequate and much easier to get.

There is a practical dividend here too. Early and late slots are less contested, which means a wider choice of specialist, which for a Higher Level subject is the difference that matters. A family willing to take 16:30 or 20:30 will usually be offered a stronger tutor than one insisting on 18:30, because they are choosing from a larger pool. The table sets out what each slot is good for and who it fits.

sections.heading: Gulf Standard Time and the tutor pool: who is awake at 19:00 in Dubai
paragraphs: Dubai runs on Gulf Standard Time, four hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time, with no daylight saving change through the year. That single fact decides which tutors can teach a Dubai evening, and it is the piece of arithmetic nobody publishes. A 19:00 Dubai slot is 15:00 in London, 20:30 in Mumbai, 23:00 in Singapore and 11:00 in Toronto. A 16:30 Dubai slot is 12:30 in London, which is lunchtime for a working teacher and therefore harder to get than families assume.

The consequence is counter-intuitive. Later Dubai evenings, which parents often treat as a compromise, are frequently better covered than early ones, because they fall in the afternoon or early evening of the time zones where many subject specialists are based. A Dubai family taking 19:00 or 20:00 is drawing on tutors in the United Kingdom, Europe and South Asia who are working a normal day. A family insisting on 16:30 is drawing on a smaller pool, and will usually be offered fewer options.

Daylight saving matters at the margins. Dubai does not change its clocks; the United Kingdom and Europe do, twice a year. A slot agreed in October with a London-based tutor shifts by an hour relative to their day in late March, which is usually invisible but occasionally breaks a fixed arrangement at exactly the wrong moment in the Diploma calendar. It is worth confirming the slot survives both clock changes when a two-year arrangement is being set up.

sections.heading: Why a 21:00 session is usually a poor purchase
paragraphs: Because the work does not survive the night. A Diploma student who finishes a tutoring hour at 22:00, then showers, messages friends and goes to bed at midnight, has given the new material no consolidation time at all. The session felt productive, the tutor was good, and by Thursday the method has gone. Parents then conclude that the subject is the problem or the tutor is, when the actual problem was the time on the clock.

There is a second cost that matters more in the Diploma than in any earlier stage. Sleep debt accumulates across a two-year programme, and a student short of sleep loses exactly the capacities the IB assesses: working memory under time pressure, sustained written argument, and accuracy in the final third of a long paper. Adding a late session to a week that is already short of sleep makes the examined performance worse while making the family feel more prepared.

So the honest position is that late slots should be rare, short and used for the right work. Reviewing a script already marked, planning the next week, choosing an exhibition object, talking through a research question: these survive a late hour. New content, timed practice and anything requiring sustained concentration do not. A tutor who takes a 21:00 booking for first-time teaching of a Higher Level topic without saying this is prioritising the booking over the outcome. If the only slot a family can offer is 21:00, the better plan is a shorter session twice a week or a weekend morning, and that is worth saying before the first invoice rather than after the third.

sections.heading: What a single evening hour fixes in each Diploma subject
paragraphs: The useful question before booking is not what does my child need help with, but what can be finished in sixty minutes. Those are different questions and the second one produces a plan. Most Diploma problems decompose into one-hour pieces: one technique, one question type, one criterion, one section of a draft. The pieces that do not decompose, a full timed paper, a complete internal assessment review, a Paper 1 simulation, need a longer sitting and should be booked as one.

The table below is the decomposition for the subjects Dubai families most often book. Read the third column as a warning rather than a limitation: it names the things that will fail if they are attempted in an evening hour, which is the most common way an otherwise good tutoring arrangement produces nothing. A student half way through a two-hour paper when the hour ends has learned less than one who did six questions properly.

The same logic applies to the week rather than the hour. Two subjects on two evenings works. Two subjects in one evening does not, because the second hour of concentration on a school night produces notes rather than learning. Three evenings a week is the practical ceiling for a Diploma student who also has homework in six subjects, and families who go beyond it usually find the homework suffering, which costs more than the tutoring gains. Where a student genuinely needs four subjects supported, the right answer is a weekend block and two evenings rather than four evenings, because the fourth evening comes out of sleep.

sections.heading: The evening hour against the drive to a tuition centre
paragraphs: The alternative most Dubai families actually consider is not another online tutor; it is a tuition centre in Al Barsha, Karama or Jumeirah with a 18:30 group class. The comparison that matters there is not the hourly rate but the total time the evening costs. A 90-minute class with 25 minutes of driving each way, in the evening peak on Sheikh Zayed Road or Al Khail Road, is two hours and twenty minutes of a school night for 90 minutes of group teaching in which a student may ask two questions.

An online one-to-one hour costs sixty minutes of the evening and delivers sixty minutes of attention directed at one student's actual losses. That is the entire argument, and it is an arithmetic argument rather than a quality claim. A good centre teacher may well be better than a mediocre online tutor; what a centre cannot give a Diploma student is an hour in which every question asked is their own and every piece of work marked is theirs.

Group classes still have a place. They are cheaper per hour, they suit content delivery where a whole cohort has the same gap, and some students work better with others in the room. The honest comparison is in the table: what each option costs in time and money, and what it is genuinely good at. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai, so the in-home column is included as market context rather than as something we sell.

sections.heading: Where the marks actually go, and which evening objectives recover them
paragraphs: Across Diploma subjects the losses cluster in four places, and three of the four are repairable in evening hours. The first is form: working not shown, units dropped, significant figures wrong, axes unlabelled, state symbols missing. The second is question reading: answering the topic rather than the command term. The third is the internal assessment, where the criteria rewarding evaluation and reflection are written last and thinnest. The fourth is genuine content absence, which is the one an hour a week struggles with.

Form losses are the cheapest to recover and the most neglected, because they feel beneath attention. A student who drops units twice a paper is giving away marks they earned, and one evening hour spent marking their own last three scripts for that single fault usually ends it. Question reading takes about three sessions: list every question by command term, then answer five of the same command term in a row across different topics until the shape of the answer becomes automatic.

Internal assessment criteria are the highest-value evening work in Year 12. One hour with the published criteria and a draft section in front of the student, asking which band this currently sits in and what the band above requires, changes the mark more than a month of content revision. The student makes every change themselves; a tutor who edits the draft has created a malpractice risk that falls on the candidate, not on the tutor.
